More questions related to this data...

To determine the best detection function to use in my models I ranked my null model using each of the four available functions (halfnorm, hazard, exp, and uniform).  The models rank however it gives a warning message "In sqrt (diag(vcov(x,altNames = TRU))) : NaNs produced.  Anyway, the best model was uniform however as John pointed out there is no detection output for that function (and I would like to report an estimate of detection ) so I switched my models to include the next best ranked detection function which was the exp function however when I use backTransform the detection estimate is 15761, SE=88712.  If I use halfnorm the detection estimate comes out with a similarly large number with huge SE.  As John noted, if I specify a hazard rate detection function backTransform will produce an extremely low estimate with NaN listed for the SE.

First, does anyone know what the error means when I rank my detection function models? 

Second, can anyone explain why I am having this problem with the detection function?  I can see by looking at the data that there are a large number of one time detections at each of the sites so the detection rates are very low...


Thank you.

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: gdissamp detection estimate issue
parts:
That warning, I think, means the model is not effectively converging  (sparse data as a culprit makes sense given your description), and the comparisons using AIC aren't valid.  One thing you could try is increasing the number of times the computer guesses and checks (increasing maxit, more useful in my limited experience), or iteratively fitting the model using starts from a previous fit until it converges.  The default for most algorithms is 100 iterations, maybe 500(?) for Nelder-Mead, but you can bump it up to as many as you need.  I find this warning comes up quite a bit with encounter histories that are discretized pretty finely (like, camera traps with 20 or 50 or 100 daily occasions and a lot of zeroes). 

I don't know why a uniform detection function doesn't result in a coefficient (is the assumption that detection given availability and existence is uniformly 1 out to the edge of the distance bins?).  But maybe a more useful presentation of the detection output is a plot of detection decay over distance?

messages.author: 403be63af7ebf220
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: gdissamp detection estimate issue
parts:
As John indicated, if the uniform model is the most supported then detection probability doesn't decrease with distance (over the specified distance interval). In this case, there is no detection parameter to estimate. The assumption is that p=1, or equivalently sigma=Inf. Also note that, with repeated visits and a uniform detection function, gdistsamp should return the same results as a binomial N-mixture model applied to the total counts from each visit. 

Richard
